source.title: Negligible in Size, Significant in Effect: On Scale Vectors in Large Language Models
source.authors: Mingze Wang; Shuchen Zhu; Yuxin Fang; Binghui Li; Kai Shen; Shu Zhong

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some figure values are not provided numerically in the text.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports fitted validation-loss scaling comparisons across model sizes and compute, a different experimental setup from the original scaling-law studies.
record.gate_note: The scaling-law figures and the text describing their fitted trends are included. The paper's other experiments compare scale-vector designs, weight decay, and training configurations; they are not rows for the scaling-law claim. Claims about scaling laws cited from other work are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The paper studies scale vectors in normalization layers. Its scaling-law plots (Figs 6–7) only serve to compare the authors' unified strategy against a tuned baseline. It reports no exponents, fit equations or goodness of fit for the baseline, and does not ask whether loss follows a power law. The fitted curve is used as a tool to argue the method's gains persist at larger scale, so this is T4 rather than a test of V1. Each size also trains on about 100 tokens per parameter, so tokens are not held non-bottleneck.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The paper's main conclusion is that scale vectors, though negligible in size, substantially affect pre-training through optimization (preconditioning) rather than expressivity. Weight decay should be applied to Input-Norm but not Output-Norm scale vectors. A unified strategy (HG+DNP+OR+IWD) consistently lowers terminal loss versus tuned baselines, and fitted scaling curves suggest the gains may persist at larger scale.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies scale-vector interventions and compares fitted loss-versus-compute trends; it does not reproduce the original scaling-law or compute-optimal-allocation methodology.

fits_no_version.finding: A normalization scale-vector redesign gives a slightly steeper fitted loss-vs-compute slope than the baseline for MoE models (no numeric slope given). It is also described as more favorable for dense models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Small optimization-related architecture changes can alter the fitted compute-scaling slope of pretraining loss, not just its offset.

record.problems: The scaling-law plots do not provide numerical fit equations, exponents, uncertainty estimates, or detailed fitting procedures in the text. The tested model-size and compute ranges are limited relative to the claim's several-orders-of-magnitude scope.
record.rows_left_out: No additional scaling-law rows were left out. The per-model training-loss curves and unrelated scale-vector ablations were not catalogued as separate scaling-law findings; the scaling-law evidence is the aggregate fitted compute plots in Figures 6–7.

untested.parts: No exponents, fit quality or several-orders-of-magnitude range. Parameters and tokens are not separated.
No depth/width variation at fixed parameter count.
No comparison of fitting choices or of setup effects on exponents.

record.verdict_notes: Scaling-law evidence is incidental: the curves are used to compare methods. No numbers are given beyond the efficiency multipliers 1.22× (dense) and 1.25× (MoE) in the figures. Fig 10 (0.033 loss gain at matched parameter count) concerns normalization design, not the depth/width shape that V4 names, so it was not linked. Because the paper is not a test, no verdict labels are given.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not report exponents or fit details, test a several-orders-of-magnitude range, or isolate parameter count and training tokens while holding the other quantities non-bottleneck.
No small-run fit is evaluated against the loss of a held-out, orders-of-magnitude-larger run.
No compute-budget sweep selects a loss-minimising parameter/token allocation.
No comparison varies depth, width, or architecture details at fixed parameter count to test their effect on loss.
The experiments concern language-model pretraining; other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer are not tested.
No downstream task performance is measured.
The paper does not compare fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocations across fitting choices or training setups, or report curves bending away from a single power law.
